active-recall-test-yourself.title: Active Recall: Close the Notes and Make Memory Work
active-recall-test-yourself.subtitle: Retrieve first, check second — and do not confuse remembering a rule with being able to use it
active-recall-test-yourself.description: Before rereading, hide the source and try to produce the answer from memory. Then check it, fix the misses, and practice application separately if the real goal is solving, speaking, writing, or doing. Familiarity feels nice; retrieval tells you what is actually available without the page in front of you.
active-recall-test-yourself.reason: Retain the bounded retrieval-practice evidence while rewriting the reviewed protocol in Brali's explanatory voice. The page now teaches the difference between familiarity, retrieval, and application; removes inherited unsupported precision; and uses dry humor only to challenge learning theatre, not the reader. A 2021 systematic review supports retrieval practice for classroom learning/retention; two 2026 sources narrow interpretation by distinguishing direct and forward testing effects and showing that improved rule retention did not automatically produce better rule application in one classroom study.
forbidden_public_fragments: improved recall accuracy from roughly 60% to 85%
Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Close the source and try to retrieve the target information from memory before looking. Check the answer and correct errors. If the real goal is application, follow recall with a task that requires actual application.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Hide the source and answer a question, explain the idea, or write what you remember. Check immediately enough to catch errors and repair them. Then, if success means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, practice that outcome too. Memory practice is useful; it is not a teleportation device to skill.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What could I retrieve without looking? What was missing or wrong? If the real goal is application, could I actually use the knowledge in a relevant task?
lifeOsSource.reference: Agarwal, Nunes & Blunt (2021) — systematic review of retrieval practice in schools and classrooms

references.title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
references.claim_scope: Supports retrieval practice as a useful learning strategy across 50 applied classroom experiments coded in the review. The review concerned educational learning outcomes and was geographically narrow: only a small minority of experiments were conducted outside the United States and Western Europe.

references.title: Research on the testing effect routinely conflates direct and forward testing effects: A meta-analysis of testing effects with free recall
references.claim_scope: Shows that the literature commonly called the testing effect mixes direct benefits for tested material with forward effects on subsequently learned material. In this free-recall meta-analysis, 66% of included effects came from mixed designs and 34% from direct designs, so Brali avoids treating one broad testing-effect label as a single outcome or mechanism.

references.title: Mixed effects of retrieval practice on the acquisition of procedural knowledge in verb spelling education
references.claim_scope: In a cluster-randomized classroom study of 105 fourth-grade pupils learning Dutch verb-spelling rules, adding retrieval practice to worked examples improved rule retention after one week but did not outperform worked examples alone on correct rule application. This supports separating retention from application, not a universal claim about all procedural skills.

faq.question: What is active recall?
faq.answer: It means trying to retrieve information from memory before looking at the answer, then checking and correcting. A question, a blank page, a flashcard cue, or a short explanation can all create that retrieval attempt.

faq.question: Is rereading useless?
faq.answer: No. Reading gives you information; retrieval checks whether you can produce it without the source. Worked examples, reading, feedback, retrieval, and application practice can solve different parts of the learning problem. Declaring one of them the One True Method would be convenient, but the evidence is less theatrical.

faq.question: If I can recall the rule, can I assume I can apply it?
faq.answer: No. Remembering and applying are different outcomes. A 2026 classroom study found better long-term retention of spelling rules when retrieval practice was added to worked examples, but no superior rule application compared with worked examples alone. If application matters, practice application directly.

faq.question: How long should an active-recall session be?
faq.answer: Brali does not prescribe a universal evidence-backed timer. Use a set small enough that you can retrieve, check, and correct carefully. Twenty-five, thirty, or forty-two minutes do not become scientific merely because a timer can count them.

intro.html: Rereading feels productive because the page keeps supplying the answer. Everything looks familiar, which is pleasant but not the same thing as being able to retrieve it later. Active recall changes the task: hide the answer, try to produce it, then check. Applied classroom research supports retrieval practice for learning and retention. The useful boundary is just as important: remembering a rule does not automatically mean you can use it in a new problem. So Brali separates retrieval from application instead of asking one technique to perform two jobs.

sections.title: 1. First decide what game you are playing
sections.html: Do you need to remember something, use it, or both? If the exam asks for a definition, retrieval is close to the target. If the job is to solve a case, speak a language, debug code, or perform a procedure, recall is only one layer. Write the real outcome down before choosing the practice. Otherwise it is very easy to become excellent at flashcards and mysteriously average at the thing the flashcards were supposed to support.

sections.title: 2. Close the source. Yes, actually close it.
sections.html: Use a question, cue, blank page, flashcard prompt, or short explanation task. Try to produce the target information before revealing it. A failed retrieval is not a verdict on your intelligence; it is a diagnostic signal that the answer was not available on demand yet. That is much more useful than another pass where the page politely does the remembering for you.

sections.title: 3. Check before the mistake becomes a souvenir
sections.html: Compare your response with the source soon enough to catch omissions and errors. Repair them explicitly: write the missing step, restate the definition, or explain why your answer was wrong. The practical loop is retrieve → check → correct. Repeated guessing without feedback is not active recall with extra courage; it is just unresolved error.

sections.title: 4. Remembering is not doing. Annoying, but useful.
sections.html: If knowing the answer is not the final goal, now use the knowledge. Solve a fresh problem, write a sentence, classify a new example, perform the procedure, or explain how the rule changes a real decision. A 2026 classroom study found that adding retrieval practice to worked examples improved retention of spelling rules after one week without improving correct rule application beyond worked examples alone. The lesson is not that retrieval failed. It is that the outcome changed.

sections.title: 5. Repeat the weak spots, not the whole textbook out of superstition
sections.html: Return later to material you want to keep accessible, especially items you missed or could only partly retrieve. Space those opportunities when useful. Brali does not prescribe a sacred number of questions, repetitions, minutes, or percentage targets. Track whether retrieval is becoming more reliable and whether the separate application task is improving.

sections.title: 6. Keep the claim as specific as the evidence
sections.html: A 2026 meta-analysis points out that research grouped under the broad label testing effect often mixes direct benefits for tested material with forward effects on material learned later. That does not weaken the basic practice; it stops us from using one impressive label for several different outcomes. When you describe what worked, say whether you mean remembering the tested material, learning later material, or applying knowledge. Precision is less exciting than magic. It is also more reusable.

sections.title: 7. Run one small learning loop
sections.html: Pick three to five things you genuinely need to retain. Retrieve them without looking, check the misses, and correct them. Then choose one application task if the real goal requires performance. At the next normal study session, ask two questions: Can I still retrieve it? and Can I use it? Keep the parts that improve the outcome you actually care about; change the rest.
